newsitem.title: USA: Jury ends first day of deliberations in McVeigh case.
newsitem.headline: Jury ends first day of deliberations in McVeigh case.

text.p: Jurors began deciding Timothy McVeigh's fate on Thursday after prosecutors said the Oklahoma city bomber deserved to die and the defence pleaded for his life, saying otherwise he would take his secrets to the grave.
The jury ended their first day of deliberations without reaching a conclusion. The judge excused them for the day and told the jury to have some rest and return on Friday.
Earlier in a surprising admission, chief defence attorney Stephen Jones appeared to concede that McVeigh was guilty of the Oklahoma City bombing that killed 168 people.

"He is not a demon, though surely his act was demonic," Jones said in his closing statement, before the jury began deliberating whether the 29-year-old Gulf War veteran should be sentenced to death by lethal injection or life in prison without parole for the worst mass murder in U.S. history.

But Jones urged the jury to spare McVeigh's life, saying that if he was executed the full story of the April 19, 1995 bombing may never be known and other possible conspirators never brought to justice.
"Dead men do not tell tales. The government may not be the only people who want my client executed," Jones said, implying that others would be glad to see McVeigh take his secret to the grave.
"The book of the Oklahoma City bombing is not closed ... Do not close it. Do not permit others to close it. Let there be a full accounting," he said.
Jones has suggested throughout the trial that other people were involved in the bomb plot, at one point saying the real bomber may have died in the blast.
Chief prosecutor Joe Hartzler dismissed Jones' tactic as a "tease." "Don't speculate on what may happen in the future. We're never going to hear from him. Forget about that," Hartzler said.

Prosecutors urged the jury of seven men and five women to have no mercy on McVeigh. "Look into the eyes of a coward and tell him you will have courage," prosecutor Beth Wilkinson said during a hard-hitting 35-minute speech. "Tell him he is no patriot. He is a traitor and he deserves to die."
"It's time, it's time for justice," she told the jurors who 10 days ago found McVeigh guilty of the bombing.

Hartzler was almost apologetic about asking the jury to send a man to his death. "I'm sorry to have to ask you to do this. I'm sorry you have to do it, but you do," he said in a hushed voice. McVeigh betrayed no emotion and the jurors looked serious.

Jones hinted there could be more violence if McVeigh was executed, saying the jury could take a first step to restoring "domestic tranquillity" by sparing his life. "It's time for this madness to end, it's time to reconcile," he said.
Hartzler described that argument as "a terrorist threat, it's pure intimidation."

After instructing the jurors on the law, federal Judge Richard Matsch sent the jurors off to begin deliberations. "The law requires you to approach the sentencing decision with an open mind," Matsch said. He did not sequester them as he had after the first phase of the trial.
The jury ended the first day of deliberations on Thursday without reaching a decision on McVeigh's fate.

Before leaving the courtroom, McVeigh looked at his mother, Mildred Frazer, who was in court with his father Bill and sister Jennifer. His mother waved to him and he nodded before being escorted out by U.S. marshals. McVeigh's parents pleaded for their son's life when they testified on Wednesday.
Wilkinson stressed the enormity of McVeigh's crime, saying the bombing was "the most bloody domestic terrorist act in the history of our country."
She said McVeigh killed more Americans on a single day than were killed in combat in the Gulf War. "There would not be enough seats in this courtroom if we could bring them all back today."

Defence lawyers said all Americans were partly to blame for the Oklahoma City bombing because the country failed to respond adequately to federal sieges at Ruby Ridge, Idaho in 1992 and at Waco, Texas in 1993 that became rallying cries for the right-wing. "We all bear some responsibility for Oklahoma City," defence attorney Richard Burr said.

The defence has said McVeigh was deeply disturbed by the deaths of 80 Branch Davidian cult members in a confrontation with federal agents at Waco. Prosecutors said he bombed the Murrah building to avenge their deaths.
McVeigh was found guilty on June 2 of 11 murder, conspiracy and bombing charges, all of which carry a possible death penalty.
